title: Wage board sets garment minimum wage at Tk 17,000 after vote
excerpt: The board voted 4-2 in the early hours of Wednesday for a Tk 17,000 entry-level wage, up 36% from Tk 12,500. Workers' representatives voted against.

image.alt: File photo: workers at sewing machines in a garment factory in Dhaka
image.credit: File photo: Kroisenbrunner / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

content:
The Minimum Wage Board for the garment sector has set the minimum monthly wage for entry-level workers at Tk 17,000, the Financial Express reported. The decision came in the early hours of Wednesday (25 November), after a meeting that began at 2pm on Tuesday (24 November) at the board's Segunbagicha office in Dhaka. The Daily Star reported that the meeting ended at about 2am.

The new figure is Tk 4,500, or 36%, above the current minimum of Tk 12,500, set in 2023. Owners and workers could not agree, so board chairman Syed Azad Subhani put the matter to a vote, the Financial Express reported, citing sources at the meeting. Babul Akhter, the workers' representative on the board, told The Daily Star that four of the six members voted for Tk 17,000 and two backed a workers' proposal of Tk 18,000. According to the Financial Express, the chairman, the independent member and two owners' representatives voted in favour, and the two workers' representatives voted against.

The board also set wages for higher grades: Tk 21,500 for grade 1, Tk 20,000 for grade 2 and Tk 19,200 for grade 3, according to wage board office data reported by The Daily Star and the Financial Express. The Business Standard reported the grade 3 figure as Tk 19,000; Devlens has used the board's figure.

The Business Standard reported that the rate still needs approval from the labour and employment ministry, which can raise it before issuing the official notification, and that it is expected to apply to work from December. It said the 36% rise is the smallest percentage increase since the first garment wage structure in 1986.

Protests continued on Tuesday. Workers blocked the Dhaka-Tangail and Dhaka-Mymensingh highways in Gazipur and clashed with police, the Financial Express reported. Gazipur Industrial Police Superintendent Md Amjad Hossain said 70 factories declared a one-day holiday, in addition to 32 already shut indefinitely under the labour law's 'no work, no pay' provision. The Business Standard, citing the BGMEA, said production was suspended at 481 factories. More than 100 members of labour groups, including the Sammilito Garments Sramik Federation and Garments Sramik Sanghati, protested outside the wage board office demanding Tk 30,000.

Why it matters

The wage will set pay for about the next three years for workers in the country's largest export industry, most of them women. Workers' groups had asked for Tk 30,000 and their board representatives voted against the final figure, so the decision may not end the unrest that has shut hundreds of factories this month. For NGOs working on women's livelihoods, legal aid and labour rights, both the size of the rise and how it is enforced at factory level matter.

What to watch

Whether the labour ministry approves the rate unchanged or raises it, when the gazette notification is issued, and how trade unions respond. Watch also whether factories reopen and December wages are paid at the new rate.
